Problem Set 2

Author

Khalid Khogali

Published

October 16, 2026

GitHub repo: https://github.com/KhalidKho/ec422_ps2_Khogali

Data

These are seasonally adjusted monthly unemployment rates for the United States, Oregon, California, Texas, and New York. The data come from FRED and are saved locally.

unemp_raw <- read_rds("data/unemp_raw.rds")

knitr::kable(
  head(unemp_raw),
  caption = "First six rows of the data"
)
First six rows of the data
symbol date price
UNRATE 1976-01-01 7.9
UNRATE 1976-02-01 7.7
UNRATE 1976-03-01 7.6
UNRATE 1976-04-01 7.7
UNRATE 1976-05-01 7.4
UNRATE 1976-06-01 7.6 
The sample covers January 1976 through September 2026.

Wrangling

I renamed the rate column and added region names. Following the instructions, I replaced October 2025 rates with September’s values. I also calculated each region’s monthly change in percentage points.

Full sample

Mean, minimum, and maximum unemployment rates for each region:

knitr::kable(
  unemp_summary,
  digits = 2,
  col.names = c("Region", "Mean (%)", "Minimum (%)", "Maximum (%)")
)
Region Mean (%) Minimum (%) Maximum (%)
California 7.07 3.8 16.1
New York 6.35 3.8 16.7
Oregon 6.66 3.4 13.7
Texas 5.85 3.4 12.8
United States 6.05 3.4 14.8

Largest increases excluding 2020

The five largest monthly increases, including ties. Changes are measured in percentage points.

unemp_top_increases_no_covid |>
  select(region, date, unemployment_rate, unemployment_rate_change) |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 2,
    col.names = c("Region", "Month", "Rate (%)", "Change (pp)")
  )
Region Month Rate (%) Change (pp)
Texas 2009-05-01 7.6 1.1
Oregon 2008-12-01 8.9 0.7
Oregon 2008-11-01 8.2 0.7
Oregon 2009-01-01 9.6 0.7
Oregon 1980-03-01 7.4 0.6
United States 1980-04-01 6.9 0.6

Largest decreases excluding 2020

The five largest monthly decreases, including ties. Negative values mean unemployment fell.

  )

Visualization

Unemployment by region

This graph compares all five regions over time.

Separate region graphs

Separate panels make each region easier to follow. They use the same scale for comparison.

Average unemployment

Regions are ordered from lowest to highest average unemployment over the full sample.

Oregon and the United States

I chose to compare Oregon with the national rate since 2015 because I wanted to see how unemployment here compares with the country overall. Using just two lines makes the differences easier to see.

Reflection

I used AI to teach me how to write some code and trouble shoot the code I was writing initially. But making the graphs was simple once I had the data ready. I wasn’t sure when to run each block of code. I also had trouble with Git because I hadn’t saved my changes before trying to commit them. I learned that saving, committing, and pushing are separate steps. I feel more comfortable using Git now and checking that my work shows up on GitHub.
